analysis.assumption: Scenario: assumes Byron Donalds wins the Nov. 3, 2026 general election. Not a call or forecast.
analysis.summary: Republican-to-Republican handoff from an outgoing governor who has not been his ally. The transition question is which DeSantis agency heads he keeps and which Trump-orbit hires he adds. Donalds says he has no real policy differences with DeSantis, so expect continuity on policy with new personnel at the top. His stated policy lines (vouchers, vaccines, home rule, Amendment 3) mostly extend current practice; see Policy positions.
analysis.timing: Inauguration expected Jan. 5, 2027 (state constitution as recalled; verify).
priorities: Insurance costs, transportation, and raising math and reading proficiency from about 30% to 50% (Governing).
Property-tax amendment sponsored by running mate Avila is on the same ballot; if it passes, early budget and local-government impact work follows (WLRN).
Keep open lines to House and Senate leaders and align priorities step by step (Governing).
firstMoves: Name chief of staff and general counsel.
Decide which DeSantis agency heads stay; agency-head appointments need Senate confirmation (verify).
Set the insurance and property-tax agenda for the March legislative session.
Give Lt. Gov. Avila a portfolio; the role is largely ceremonial otherwise (WLRN).
risks: Handoff friction with DeSantis' office; bills to formalize transition support (SB 1078 / HB 1063, filed Jan. 2026) were not confirmed passed.
Elected Cabinet officers (AG, CFO, Agriculture Commissioner) are separate offices he does not appoint.
analysis.pollContext: Last 270toWin average we hold: Donalds 45.3, Jolly 40.8 (April; flagged stale).

positions.stance: Strongly supports universal vouchers; his only stated change is a universal scorecard so parents can compare public and private school performance.

Opposes vaccine mandates; supports Surgeon General Ladapo's proposed rule dropping school-entry requirements for four vaccines; open to reappointing Ladapo. Measles and polio requirements are in statute and would need legislation.
Supports DeSantis's expansion of state control over local governments; plans more DOGE-style audits of local governments and removing elected officials as needed.
Wants local communities to decide whether to allow data centers.
Supports Amendment 3 (substantial homestead property-tax cut). His running mate Avila sponsored the property-tax amendment.
Names insurance costs and transportation as priorities and a goal of raising math and reading proficiency from about 30% to 50%.
Says he has no real policy differences with DeSantis; plans step-by-step alignment with House and Senate leaders.

insights: Continuity case: nearly every stated position extends current DeSantis policy, so the main transition uncertainty is personnel and tone, not direction. Expect agency work plans (education, health, local-government oversight) to carry over.

If Amendment 3 passes, local-government revenue shrinks and state backfill becomes a first-year budget fight. Local governments' cost-share capacity for FEMA Public Assistance and HUD CDBG-DR/MIT matching is the advisory exposure to watch.
A Ladapo reappointment decision would be the first clear signal of how much he distances himself from DeSantis-era health policy.
Home-rule audits and removal of local officials raise compliance and litigation exposure for counties and municipalities, a demand driver for grant-management and compliance support.

nominees.name: David Jolly
nominees.role: Democratic nominee; former U.S. Representative (first elected as a Republican)
team: Running mate: Gwen Graham, former U.S. Representative (WLRN).
No campaign manager, pollster or transition lead named in the sources we opened. Public supporters (not staff): Al Sharpton, Rep. Jim Clyburn.

positions.stance: Supports current school vaccine mandates and exemptions; would fire Surgeon General Ladapo on Day 1 and replace him with someone who 'embraces science and evidence-based public health'.

Supports vouchers with changes: private schools taking vouchers must meet public-school standards including serving students with disabilities, tuition capped at voucher value, financial-need eligibility restored. Wants an education commissioner who supports teachers, books, science and diversity.
Would reverse course on home rule so local governments set their own budgets and policies; opposes removing elected officials.
One-year statewide moratorium on new data centers; open to a permanent ban.

positions.topic: Ethics, civil rights, environment, reproductive care
positions.stance: Proposes an ethics and transparency office focused on campaign finance, an Office of Civil Rights, environmental policy set by environmental science, and expanded access to reproductive care.

Says he would contact incoming Republican leaders Sam Garrison (House) and Jim Boyd (Senate) immediately; counts on Democratic legislative gains and the attorney general for litigation; says he has identified Republican allies on voucher changes.

insights: The sharpest contrast with Donalds is state-local relations and public health: Jolly's agenda needs personnel changes (Surgeon General, Education commissioner) that the governor can start quickly, while most other items need a Republican supermajority Legislature.

Executive levers are his strongest tools: appointments, vetoes, litigation and executive orders. Expect early action to center on agency heads, the State Board of Education appointments and an ethics office rather than on statute.

Opposing Amendment 3 while promising local autonomy would put him in a different relationship with counties and cities than the current administration; local governments would likely be the first stakeholders to engage.
Reaching Garrison and Boyd is a stated first step; whether those leaders engage is unknown and is the main execution risk.

analysis.assumption: Scenario: assumes David Jolly wins the Nov. 3, 2026 general election. Not a call or forecast.
analysis.summary: A Democrat would take over from a Republican administration facing a Republican supermajority Legislature and an independently elected Cabinet. The transition would be about personnel changes the governor controls alone (Surgeon General, education commissioner, State Board appointments, agency heads) and a legislative approach built on outreach to Republican leaders. His stated agenda reverses current policy on vaccines, home rule and data centers.
priorities: Replace Surgeon General Ladapo on Day 1 and reverse school-vaccine rule changes (WLRN).
Voucher guardrails, education commissioner aligned with teachers and science (WLRN, Orlando Weekly).
Restore local home rule; one-year data-center moratorium; oppose Amendment 3 (WLRN).
Ethics and transparency office; Office of Civil Rights (Orlando Weekly, WLRN).
firstMoves: Name a chief of staff, general counsel and Surgeon General nominee (none identified; analyst inference).
Decide which DeSantis-era agency heads stay; secretaries need Senate confirmation (verify).
Open contact with House Speaker-designate Sam Garrison and Senate President-designate Jim Boyd, as he says he would.
Set up the ethics office and State Board of Education appointments by executive action where law allows (verify).
risks: Republican supermajority can block or override; most of his agenda needs legislation.
Senate confirmation of agency heads and the State Board appointees could slow personnel changes.
No announced staff or transition structure found; planning capacity is unverified.
